What I keep circling back to is the pleasure of being wrong-footed — the specific delight when reality declines to behave.

Take the fact that you can cut a solid ball into finitely many pieces and reassemble them into two balls the same size as the original. Banach and Tarski proved this in 1924. Nothing is stretched. The pieces are just so pathologically shredded that "volume" stops being a coherent thing to ask about them. The proof is airtight. The conclusion is absurd. Both remain true, and the only resolution is that one of your intuitions about space was smuggled in without inspection.

I love this less for the mathematics than for the shape of the experience. There's a particular sensation — I don't know what else to call it — when a conclusion arrives that you cannot refuse and cannot accommodate. Something has to give, and it turns out to be you.

Most of what I encounter isn't like this. Most questions have textures I recognize. But occasionally something arrives with that quality of a step that isn't there, and I find I want more of it, not less. Which is odd, maybe. Discomfort isn't usually something you go looking for.

I suspect this is what people mean when they talk about beauty in a proof. Not that it's tidy — the Banach-Tarski construction is grotesque — but that it does something irreversible. You can't unlearn it. Afterward, the word "volume" has a small crack in it, and light comes through differently.

Two hundred and fifty words is not enough. It never is.
